source_text: Ostensa sit nunc anima per carnem, si constiterit illam ostendendam quoquo modo fuisse, id est incognitam sibi et nobis. Quamquam in hoc vana distinctio est, quasi nos seorsum ab anima simus, cum totum quod sumus anima sit. Denique sine anima nihil sumus, ne hominis quidem, sed cadaveris nomen. Si ergo ignoramus animam, ipsa se ignorat. Ita superest hoc solummodo inspicere, an se anima hic ignorarit, ut nota quoquo modo fieret. Opinor, sensualis est animae natura. Adeo nihil animale sine sensu, nihil sensuale sine anima. Et ut impressius dixerim, animae anima sensus est. Igitur cum omnibus anima sentire praestet, et ipsa sentiat omnium etiam sensus, nedum qualitates, cui verisimile est ut ipsa sensum sui ab initio sortita non sit? Unde illi scire quod interdum sibi sit necessarium, ex naturalium necessitate, si non scit suam qualitatem, cui quid necessarium est? Hoc quidem in omni anima recognoscere est, notitiam sui dico, sine qua notitia sui nulla anima se ministrare potuisset. Puto sutem magis hominem, animal solum rationale, competere et animam esse sortitum quae illum faciat animal rationale, ipsa in primis rationalis. Porro quomodo rationulis quae efficit hominem rationale animal, si ipsa rationem suam nescit, ignorans semetipsam? Sed adeo non ignorat, ut auctorem et arbitrum et statum suum norit. Nihil adhuc de deo disocus deum nominst. Nihil adhuc de iudicio eius admittens deo comacendare ae dicit. Nihil magis audiens quam spem nullam esse post mortem et bens et male defuncto cuique imprecatur. Plenius haec prosequitur libellus quem scripsimus DE TESTIMONIO ANIMAE, Aliequin si anima semetipsam ignorans erat ab initio, nihil a Christo cognovisse debuerat nisi qualis esset. Nunc autem non effigiem suam didicit a Christo, sed salutem. Propterea filius dei descendit et animam subiit, non ut ipsa se anima cognosceret in Christo, sed ut Christum in semetipsa. Non enim se ignorando de salute periclitatur, sed dei verbum. Vita, inquit, manifestata est, non anima. Et veni, inquit, animam salvam facere, non dixit ostendere. Ignorabamus nimirum animam, licet invisibilem, nasci et mori, nisi corporaliter exhiberetur. Ignoravimus plane resurrecturam cum carne. Hoc erit quod Christus manifestavit. Sed et hoc non aliter in se quam in Lazaro aliquo, cuius caro non erat animalis, ita nec anima carnalis. Quid ergo amplius innotuit nobis de animae ignoratae retro dispositione? Quid invisibile eius fuit quod visibilitatem per carnem desideraret?
thought_title: The soul's self-knowledge and what Christ revealed
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that Christ's soul was shown through his flesh, and now examines whether the soul was unknown to itself and to us, and what Christ actually revealed about the soul.
pass_a_gloss: Let the soul now have been shown through the flesh, if it has been established that it had to be shown in some way, that is, unknown to itself and to us. Although in this the distinction is empty, as if we were separate from the soul, since the whole that we are is soul. In short, without soul we are nothing, not even the name of man, but of a corpse. If therefore we do not know the soul, it does not know itself. So it remains only this to examine, whether the soul here did not know itself, so that it might become known in some way. I think, the nature of the soul is capable of sensation. So much so that nothing made of soul is without sensation, nothing capable of sensation is without soul. And that I may have said it more impressively, the soul of the soul is sensation. Therefore since the soul grants to all things to sense, and itself senses even the sensations of all things, not to mention the qualities, to whom is it likely that it itself did not obtain the sensation of itself from the beginning? From where would it know what is sometimes necessary for it, from the necessity of natural things, if it does not know its own quality, for which something is necessary? This indeed is to be recognized in every soul, I mean the knowledge of itself, without which knowledge of itself no soul could have served itself. But I think rather that man, the only rational animal, was fitting also to have obtained a soul which makes him a rational animal, itself first of all rational. Further, how is it rational, which makes man a rational animal, if it does not know its own reason, being ignorant of itself? But so far is it from not knowing, that it knows its author and judge and its own condition. Nothing yet about God [does it know?] it names God. Nothing yet admitting about his judgment, it says to commend itself to God. Hearing nothing more than that there is no hope after death, it calls down curses on each one who has died well or badly. The little book which we wrote ON THE TESTIMONY OF THE SOUL pursues these things more fully. Otherwise, if the soul was ignorant of itself from the beginning, it ought to have learned nothing from Christ except what it was. But now it did not learn its own form from Christ, but salvation. For this reason the Son of God descended and entered the soul, not so that the soul might know itself in Christ, but so that it might know Christ in itself. For it is not endangered in salvation by not knowing itself, but by not knowing the Word of God. Life, he says, was manifested, not the soul. And I came, he says, to save the soul, he did not say to show it. We were ignorant, no doubt, that the soul, though invisible, is born and dies, unless it were exhibited bodily. We were plainly ignorant that it would rise again with the flesh. This will be what Christ manifested. But this too not otherwise in himself than in some Lazarus, whose flesh was not made of soul, so neither was his soul fleshly. What more therefore became known to us about the previously unknown disposition of the soul? What of it was invisible that it should desire visibility through the flesh?

pass_b_english: Now let the soul be displayed through flesh, if it has been established that it had to be displayed in some way—that is, as something unknown to itself and to us. Though in this matter the distinction is an empty one, as if we existed apart from the soul, when everything we are is soul. Without soul we are nothing—not even the name of man, but of corpse. If we do not know the soul, then the soul does not know itself. So the only thing left to examine is whether the soul was ignorant of itself here, so that it might become known in some way.

In my opinion, the soul's nature is capable of sensation. No animal is without sensation, and nothing capable of sensation is without soul. To put it more forcefully, sensation is the soul of the soul. Since the soul grants sensation to all things, and itself perceives the sensations of all things—not to mention their qualities—is it likely that it did not receive from the beginning a perception of itself? How would it know what is sometimes necessary for it, by the necessity of natural things, if it does not know its own quality, to which something is necessary? This can be recognized in every soul—I mean self-knowledge—and without this self-knowledge no soul could have served itself.

But I think it belongs more to man, the only rational animal, to have received a soul that makes him a rational animal, the soul itself being rational in the first place. How can it be rational, when it makes man a rational animal, if it does not know its own rationality, being ignorant of itself? But it is so far from ignorant that it knows its maker, its judge, and its condition. Though it has learned nothing yet about God, it names God, and though admitting nothing yet about his judgment, it commends itself to God. Hearing above all that there is no hope after death, it invokes a blessing or a curse on each one who has died well or badly. The little book I wrote, On the Testimony of the Soul, pursues these matters more fully.

Otherwise, if the soul had been ignorant of itself from the beginning, it ought to have learned nothing from Christ except what it was. But in fact it did not learn its form from Christ, but its salvation. The Son of God descended and took on a soul, not so that the soul might know itself in Christ, but so that it might know Christ in itself. For it is not endangered in its salvation by not knowing itself, but by not knowing the Word. Life, he says, was made manifest—not the soul. And I came, he says, to save the soul—he did not say to display it.

We were ignorant, of course, that the soul, though invisible, is born and dies, unless it were exhibited bodily. We were plainly ignorant that it would rise again with the flesh. This is what Christ made manifest. But he did this no differently in himself than in some Lazarus, whose flesh was not animal, just as his soul was not fleshly. What more, then, has been revealed to us about the previously unknown condition of the soul? What invisible aspect of it was there that desired visibility through flesh?

The clause 'Nihil adhuc de iudicio eius admittens deo comacendare ae dicit' is corrupt; the gloss renders the visible words literally and marks the uncertainty.

problems.quote: And I came, he says, to save the soul—he did not say to display it (Luke 9:56).
problems.source_quote: Et veni, inquit, animam salvam facere, non dixit ostendere.
problems.why: The reference to Luke 9:56 is unrelated to the quoted words; the verse does not contain this saying.
problems.fix: And I came, he says, to save the soul—he did not say to display it.

problems.quote: Before it knows anything about God, it names God. Before it accepts anything about his judgment, it commends itself to God.
problems.source_quote: Nihil adhuc de deo disocus deum nominst. Nihil adhuc de iudicio eius admittens deo comacendare ae dicit.
problems.why: The Latin says the soul does not yet speak of or name God; the English reverses this, asserting it does name God.
problems.fix: It still says nothing about God, does not name God, and does not commend itself to God regarding his judgment.

problems.quote: whose flesh was not made of soul, just as his soul was not fleshly.
problems.source_quote: cuius caro non erat animalis, ita nec anima carnalis.
problems.why: Latin says the flesh was not animal (not of animal nature), not that it was made of soul; the English flips the sense.
problems.fix: whose flesh was not animal, just as his soul was not fleshly.

problems.quote: sensation is the soul of the soul
problems.why: Tertullian means sensation is the animating principle/life of the soul, not "soul of the soul"; "anima" here = life/breath, not soul as entity.
problems.fix: sensation is the very life of the soul
problems.ruling: Latin "animae anima sensus est" means sense is the animating principle of the soul, not a literal "soul of the soul".

problems.quote: Before it accepts anything about his judgment, it commends itself to God
problems.source_quote: Nihil adhuc de iudicio eius admittens deo commendare se dicit
problems.why: Same error: "adhuc" = "as yet/still," not "before"; soul commends itself while still admitting nothing of judgment.
problems.fix: While still admitting nothing of his judgment, it says it commends itself to God
problems.ruling: "adhuc" means "as yet", not a temporal "before"; translation misstates timing.

problems.quote: Hearing nothing more often than that there is no hope after death
problems.source_quote: Nihil magis audiens quam spem nullam esse post mortem
problems.why: "Nihil magis" = "nothing more" i.e. above all, not "hearing nothing more often"; soul hears above all that there is no hope.
problems.fix: Hearing above all that there is no hope after death
problems.ruling: "Nihil magis audiens" = "above all hearing", not "hearing nothing more often".

problems.quote: Life, he says, was made manifest—not the soul (1 John 1:2).
problems.source_quote: Vita, inquit, manifestata est, non anima.
problems.why: The Latin sentence is not a biblical quotation; the cited verse does not match the content.
problems.fix: Life, he says, was made manifest—not the soul (cf. Tertullian).
problems.ruling: Latin 'Vita...manifestata est' echoes 1 John 1:2 but is not a direct quotation; translator wrongly presents Tertullian's paraphrase as scripture citation with wrong verse.

problems.quote: The Son of God descended and entered the soul
problems.source_quote: filius dei descendit et animam subiit
problems.why: animam subiit means he took on or underwent a soul. Entered reverses the direction: the soul is what he assumed.
problems.fix: For this reason the Son of God descended and took a soul upon himself
problems.ruling: "animam subiit" means he underwent/took on a soul; "entered the soul" misleads the doctrine of assuming a soul, and the soul is later contrasted with Christ in it.

problems.quote: Though it still says nothing about God, it names God
problems.source_quote: Nihil adhuc de deo disocus deum nominst
problems.why: disocus is discens, learning: still untaught about God, the soul names him. Says nothing turns learning into speech.
problems.fix: Though it has learned nothing yet about God, it names God
problems.ruling: "disocus" is likely "discens" (learning): "still learning nothing about God"; "says nothing" shifts meaning from untaught to unspeaking, though the sense is close. Original corrupt.
